title: The Alphabet, Names and Origins
bigQuestion: What can a person's name, and the way they spell it, tell you about who they are and where they come from?

story.title: A Name with Two Last Names
story.kicker: A new classmate spells her full name, and the class learns why it is so long.
paragraphs: On Monday, a new student stood at the front of Señor Ramírez's class. "Me llamo Valentina Gómez Ortiz," she said (My name is Valentina Gómez Ortiz). A boy in the back whispered, "Two last names?" Valentina heard him and smiled. "Sí, dos apellidos" (Yes, two last names).

Señor Ramírez handed her a marker. "¿Cómo se escribe?" he asked (How is it spelled?). Valentina spelled her first name out loud with Spanish letter names: "ve, a, ele, e, ene, te, i, ene, a." The class wrote along. Some students wrote a b at first, because in Spanish b and v sound almost the same.

Then she explained. "Gómez es el apellido de mi papá. Ortiz es el apellido de mi mamá" (Gómez is my dad's last name. Ortiz is my mom's last name). In many Spanish-speaking families, a person carries both. At school in Chicago, her records only had room for one, so sometimes teachers called her "Valentina Ortiz" by mistake.

"¿De dónde eres?" asked Tomás (Where are you from?). "Soy de Chicago, pero mi familia es de Puebla, México" (I'm from Chicago, but my family is from Puebla, Mexico). She wrote Gómez on the board and pointed to the accent mark on the o. "No olviden el acento" (Don't forget the accent), she said, and the class laughed.
story.think: Why might it matter to Valentina that people use both of her last names and spell them with the accent?

lessons.title: Twenty-Seven Letters
lessons.mainIdea: The Spanish alphabet has 27 letters: the 26 English letters plus ñ.
reading: Picture a class roster in Spanish with the names Nuñez and Nuto. Which comes first? The Spanish *alfabeto* (alphabet) has one letter English lacks: *la eñe*, the letter ñ. It comes right after n. So Nuto comes before Nuñez, because n comes before ñ. Words with ñ get their own place in the dictionary.

The Real Academia Española (Royal Spanish Academy), called the RAE, is based in Madrid. It works with language academies across the Spanish-speaking world. In 2010 their spelling guide set the alphabet at 27 letters. Before that, many classrooms taught ch and ll as separate letters.

Today ch and ll are called digraphs, pairs of letters that make one sound. They are still used all the time, as in chocolate and llamar (to call). But they are not counted as their own letters. So in a dictionary, chico is filed under c, between words starting with ce and ci.

words.d: the alphabet — 27 letters in Spanish
the letter ñ — comes after n; sounds like ny in canyon
the letter — ¿Qué letra es? (What letter is it?)

lessons.title: The Names of the Letters
lessons.mainIdea: Each Spanish letter has a name, like be, ce, hache and jota, that you use to spell aloud.
reading: Picture spelling your email address to a receptionist in Spanish. You need the letter names. Vowels are simple: a, e, i, o, u, each said with one clear sound. Many letters add an e: *be* (b), *ce* (c), *de* (d), *ge* (g), *pe* (p), *te* (t). Others start with e: efe (f), ele (l), eme (m), ene (n), ese (s).

Some names surprise English speakers. H is *hache*, even though h is silent. J is *jota*, said with a sound from the throat. G is ge, which sounds like the Spanish j when it comes before e or i. Q is cu, R is erre, X is equis and Z is zeta.

Three letters have more than one common name. For v, many people say uve, and in much of Latin America people say ve or ve corta. W is uve doble or doble ve. Y is ye, and older speakers may call it i griega (Greek i). All of these are correct, so listen to what the speaker uses.

words.d: the letter h — silent in Spanish words like hola
the letter j — a breathy sound from the throat: jugar
the letter y — also called i griega by many speakers
the letter x — as in México

look.title: Spelling an Email Aloud
look.text:
Receptionist: ¿Cómo se escribe su correo? (How is your email spelled?)
Luis: ele, u, i, ese, jota, eme... arroba (@)... ge, eme, a, i, ele, punto (dot), ce, o, eme.
So luisjm@gmail.com is spelled with letter names, plus arroba for @ and punto for the dot.
look.prompt: Spell your first name aloud with Spanish letter names. Which letters were the hardest?

check.q: What is the Spanish name of the letter h?
check.why: The letter h is called hache, even though it makes no sound.

check.q: Someone spells "jota, o, ese, e." What name is it?
check.why: Jota, o, ese, e spells J-o-s-e. The accent would need to be said separately: e con acento.

check.q: Which letter is called equis?
check.why: Equis is x, as in México.

lessons.title: ¿Cómo Se Escribe?
lessons.mainIdea: Ask ¿Cómo se escribe? to learn how a word is spelled, and say con acento for an accent mark.
reading: Picture a new classmate named Ximena. You want to write her name on a card. You ask, *¿Cómo se escribe?* (How is it spelled? literally how is it written?). She answers, "equis, i, eme, e, ene, a." Asking is polite, and it keeps you from guessing wrong.

Spelling aloud has helpers. For a capital letter, say *mayúscula* (capital). For an accent mark, say con acento or con tilde after the letter: "e con acento." Double letters can be said as dos: "dos erres" (two r's) or "doble ere." So Ramírez is "erre mayúscula, a, eme, i con acento, erre, e, zeta."

Watch for letters that sound alike in Spanish. B and v sound almost the same, so people ask, "¿Con be o con uve?" S, z and c before e or i sound the same in most of Latin America. That is why spelling a name aloud matters, even for native speakers.

words.d: How is it spelled? — literally how is it written
the capital letter — say it before the letter: a mayúscula
with an accent mark — i con acento means í

look.title: Spelling Ramírez
look.text:
Student: ¿Cómo se escribe su apellido, profesor?
Sr. Ramírez: erre mayúscula, a, eme, i con acento, erre, e, zeta.
Student: ¿Con zeta o con ese?
Sr. Ramírez: Con zeta.
Letters: R-a-m-í-r-e-z.

check.q: What does ¿Cómo se escribe? ask?
check.why: ¿Cómo se escribe? asks how a word is written, that is, spelled.

check.q: How do you say the letter í when spelling aloud?

check.q: Why do Spanish speakers ask "¿Con be o con uve?"
choices: V is not a Spanish letter.
B and v sound almost the same in Spanish.
Uve is a kind of accent.
check.why: In Spanish, b and v sound nearly the same, so the spelling must be checked.

lessons.title: Me Llamo and ¿Cómo Te Llamas?
lessons.mainIdea: Ask ¿Cómo te llamas? (tú) or ¿Cómo se llama usted? and answer Me llamo plus your name.
reading: Picture the first minute of class. You turn to the student next to you and ask, *¿Cómo te llamas?* (What's your name? literally how do you call yourself?). She answers, *me llamo* Valentina (my name is Valentina). The verb is llamarse, to be called.

Look at the pattern. Me llamo is I call myself. Te llamas is you call yourself, for tú. Se llama is he, she or you (usted) call yourself. So you ask a teacher, "¿Cómo se llama usted?" The ending changes with the person: -o for yo, -as for tú, -a for él, ella and usted.

A common mistake is saying "Me llamo es Valentina," copying English "my name is." Llamo is already the verb, so es is extra. You can also say "Mi nombre es Valentina" (my name is Valentina) or "Soy Valentina" (I'm Valentina). All three are correct.

words.d: my name is — literally I call myself: Me llamo Tomás
What's your name? — informal, for tú
What's your name? — formal, for usted
the name, the first name — Mi nombre es Ana

look.title: Three Ways to Say Your Name

Classmate: ¿Cómo te llamas?

Teacher: ¿Cómo se llama usted?
Parent: Me llamo Rosa Díaz.
Other correct answers: Mi nombre es Leo. / Soy Leo.
Not correct: Me llamo es Leo.
look.prompt: Write the question you would ask a new classmate and the one you would ask the new principal.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Me llamo already contains the verb, so no es is needed.

check.q: How do you ask a new adult neighbor their name politely?
check.why: Use the usted form with an adult you just met: ¿Cómo se llama usted?

check.q: Which sentence does NOT mean "My name is Leo" or "I'm Leo"?
check.why: Se llama Leo means his name is Leo (or your name is Leo, with usted), not my name.

lessons.title: Two Last Names
lessons.mainIdea: Many Spanish speakers traditionally carry two last names: first the father's, then the mother's.
reading: Picture Valentina Gómez Ortiz. Her first name is Valentina. Her *apellidos* (last names, surnames) are Gómez and Ortiz. Traditionally, the first *apellido* comes from the father, and the second comes from the mother. This custom is common in Spain and much of Latin America.

Walk through it with her parents. Her father is Javier Gómez Ruiz. Her mother is Laura Ortiz Vega. Valentina takes Gómez, her father's first last name, and Ortiz, her mother's first last name. So she is Valentina Gómez Ortiz. Her brother Mateo is Mateo Gómez Ortiz too.

In daily life, many people use only the first last name: "Valentina Gómez." A mistake English speakers make is thinking the second last name is the main one, and calling her "Ms. Ortiz." In some countries, laws now let parents choose the order, so families can differ. When in doubt, ask.

words.d: the last name, surname — many people have two apellidos
the father — traditionally gives the first last name
the mother — traditionally gives the second last name

Step 2: take the mother's first apellido → Ortiz

lessons.title: Señor, Señora and Señorita
lessons.mainIdea: Use señor, señora or señorita with a last name to address adults with respect.
reading: Picture meeting your friend's mother, Laura Ortiz Vega. You want to be polite. You say, "Buenos días, señora Ortiz." *Señor* (Mr., sir) and *señora* (Mrs., ma'am) go before the last name. With two last names, use the first one: señora Ortiz, not señora Vega.

Señorita (Miss) is used for a young woman or girl. Some adults now prefer señora or just their name, so follow their lead. Written, these titles are often shortened with a capital: Sr., Sra., Srta. When you speak directly to the person, the title starts with a small letter in the middle of a sentence: "Gracias, señor Ramírez."

Teachers are often called *profesor* (male teacher) or profesora (female teacher), sometimes with the last name. In many schools students also say maestro or maestra. A common mistake is to say "señor" plus a first name to a teacher, like "señor Luis," when the school uses last names. Listen to what classmates say.

words.d: Mr., sir — señor Gómez; written Sr.
Miss — for a young woman or girl; written Srta.
the teacher — used as a title: Buenos días, profesora

lessons.title: ¿De Dónde Eres?
lessons.mainIdea: Ask ¿De dónde eres? and answer Soy de plus a city or country.
reading: Picture a new friend at a summer program. You want to know where she is from. You ask, *¿De dónde eres?* (Where are you from?). De means from, dónde means where, and eres means you are. Spanish puts de at the front of the question. English leaves "from" at the end.

She answers, *soy de* Chicago (I'm from Chicago). Soy means I am. For a city or a country, just add the name: "Soy de Puerto Rico." "Soy de Guatemala." With usted, ask "¿De dónde es usted?" The answer still starts with soy.

Two common mistakes come from English. One is "¿Dónde eres de?" with de at the end. The other is "Estoy de Chicago." For where you are from, Spanish uses ser (soy, eres, es), not estar. Dónde has an accent because it is a question word.

words.d: Where are you from? — informal; formal: ¿De dónde es usted?
I am from — Soy de Chicago
to be — used for origin: soy, eres, es

look.title: At a Summer Program
look.text:
Leo: Hola, ¿de dónde eres?
María: Soy de Chicago. Mi familia es de Guatemala. ¿Y tú?
Leo: Soy de Aurora, pero mis abuelos son de Puerto Rico. (my grandparents)
Notice: soy, es and son all come from ser, the verb for origin.
look.prompt: Answer ¿De dónde eres? for yourself, and add where one person in your family is from.

check.q: Which question is correct Spanish?
check.why: Spanish puts de first, and dónde has an accent: ¿De dónde eres?

check.q: Which answer is correct?
check.why: Origin uses ser: Soy de Chicago.

check.q: You ask an older visitor where she is from. What do you say?
check.why: With an older visitor use usted and its verb es.

lessons.title: Twenty Spanish-Speaking Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish is an official language in 20 countries across the Americas, Europe and Africa.
reading: Picture a world map with pins in every country where Spanish is an official language. You would count 20 countries. One is in North America: México. Six are in Central America: Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panamá. Two are island countries in the Caribbean: Cuba and the Dominican Republic, in Spanish la República Dominicana.

Nine are in South America: Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Perú, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay. In Europe there is España (Spain). In Africa there is Equatorial Guinea, called Guinea Ecuatorial. Notice the accents in México, Panamá, Perú and España's ñ.

Puerto Rico is not on this list of countries, because it is a territory of the United States. But Spanish is an official language there, next to English. The United States also has millions of Spanish speakers, including many families in Chicago. Each place has its own history, foods and ways of speaking.

the Dominican Republic — a Caribbean country

lessons.title: Nationalities and Agreement
lessons.mainIdea: Nationality words change for gender: mexicano, mexicana; español, española.
reading: Picture two cousins from Mexico, a boy and a girl. He says, "Soy *mexicano*." She says, "Soy mexicana." A nationality word is an adjective, and in Spanish most adjectives match the person. Words ending in -o switch to -a for a female: colombiano, colombiana; peruano, peruana.

Words ending in a consonant add -a for a female: español, española; inglés, inglesa. Notice that inglés loses its accent in inglesa. Words ending in -e stay the same for everyone: *estadounidense* (from the United States), costarricense (Costa Rican), nicaragüense. For a group, add -s or -es: mexicanos, españoles.

Two mistakes are common. English speakers capitalize nationality words, but Spanish writes them in lowercase: "Soy mexicana," not "Soy Mexicana." Country names still get a capital: México. The other mistake is using the -o form for everyone, as in "Ella es mexicano." Check who you are describing.

words.d: Mexican — -o for a male, -a for a female
Spanish (from Spain) — add -a for a female
from the United States — same form for males and females
the nationality — written in lowercase in Spanish: cubano, cubana

Pablo es de España → Pablo es español.
Lucía es de España → Lucía es española.
Sam y Mia son de Estados Unidos → Son estadounidenses.

check.why: A consonant-ending nationality adds -a for a female, and nationalities are lowercase.

check.q: Which nationality word is the same for males and females?

check.q: Which sentence has the correct capitalization?

Soy Mexicano y soy de méxico.
Soy Mexicano y soy de México.
soy mexicano y soy de méxico.
check.why: Nationalities are lowercase in Spanish, but country names are capitalized.

lessons.title: Accent Marks Change Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: A written accent can change a word's meaning: papá is dad, but papa is potato.
reading: Picture writing a birthday card: "Feliz cumpleaños, papa." Without the accent, you just wished a happy birthday to a potato. *Papá* (dad) has an accent on the last a. Papa, with no accent, means potato in much of Latin America. The accent mark, *el acento* or la tilde, changes both the stress and the meaning.

An accent shows which syllable is stressed when the normal rule does not apply. In papá, the stress falls on the end: pa-PÁ. In papa, it falls on the first syllable: PA-pa. You saw this in adiós and Gómez too. Leave the accent out, and a reader may stress the wrong part.

Some short words use an accent only to show a different meaning. Tú (you) and tu (your). Él (he) and el (the). Sí (yes) and si (if). English speakers often skip these marks because English has none. In Spanish, a missing accent is a spelling error, just like a missing letter.

words.d: the accent mark — also called la tilde; shows stress or a different meaning
dad — stress on the end; papa without the accent means potato
yes — si without the accent means if

look.title: Pairs That Differ by One Mark
look.text:
papá (dad) / papa (potato)
tú (you) / tu (your)
él (he) / el (the)
sí (yes) / si (if)
Try it: "Él es mi papá" means He is my dad. "El papa" without accents on either word would be the potato.

check.q: What does papa (no accent) mean in much of Latin America?
check.why: Papa without an accent means potato; papá with the accent means dad.

check.q: Which sentence means "Yes, he is my friend"?
check.why: Sí (yes) and él (he) both need their accent marks.

check.q: Why does Gómez have an accent mark?

check.why: The accent tells the reader where the stress falls when the normal rule would put it elsewhere.
